findings.text: In assertOpts, `if ot.NumIn() == 0 { return }` returns from the whole function instead of moving to the next option. If the first option takes no arguments, the later options are never value-compared. For example, `FunctionalOptions(NoArg(), WithX(1))` matches an actual call with `WithX(2)`, so the mock matches the wrong call.

`ot.In(i).Elem()` panics when an option's parameter is not a pointer or other Elem-able type. An example is an option of type `func(opts options)`, or a func taking a string. Elem panics on a non-Elem kind, so the mock panics instead of reporting a mismatch.

`reflect.TypeOf(actual).String()` panics with a nil pointer dereference when the actual argument is nil. For example, the code under test passes a nil options slice as an untyped nil. The same path panics if the actual argument is not a slice: when the expected options are empty, `assertOpts` calls `actualOpts.Len()` on a non-slice or nil value. Either case panics instead of producing a FAIL diff.

The mismatch message indexes `expectedNames[i]` with `i`, which here is the parameter index from the inner loop shadowing the option index. This gives the wrong option name, and it panics with an index out of range when an option has more parameters than there are options. The actual-side message also uses the expected name.

0.reason: Every option in the actual slice has the same function type, so if one takes no arguments they all do. No later value comparison can be skipped, and the mixed NoArg()/WithX example cannot happen with a real typed options slice.

1.reason: `ot.In(i).Elem()` is called on every parameter type without checking it, and reflect's `Type.Elem` panics for kinds such as struct or string. An option whose parameter is not a pointer therefore crashes the mock instead of reporting a mismatch.

2.reason: If `actual` is an untyped nil, `reflect.TypeOf(actual)` is nil and calling `.String()` on it panics. If `actual` is not a slice (for example the "(Missing)" placeholder string) and the expected options are empty, `assertOpts` calls `actualOpts.Len()` on a non-slice value and panics.

3.reason: The inner loop variable `i` (parameter index) shadows the option index, so `expectedNames[i]` picks the wrong option name and can go out of range when an option has more parameters than there are options. The actual-side message also uses `expectedNames` instead of `actualNames`.
